method: Butter and buttermilk are the two halves of the cream, so both the weight and the milkfat have to add up: butter plus buttermilk equals the cream weight, and butter times its fat percentage plus buttermilk times its fat percentage equals the cream weight times the cream's fat percentage. Solving those two equations for the butter weight gives cream times (cream fat minus buttermilk fat) over (butter fat minus buttermilk fat), with every percentage taken as a fraction; the buttermilk is the rest of the cream and the fat each half carries is reported so the balance can be checked. Cream weight is accepted in grams, ounces (28.349523125 g) or pounds (453.59237 g) and converted to grams first. Defaults are 1,000 g of 36 percent heavy cream churning into butter at 82 percent milkfat and buttermilk at 0.5 percent, which gives about 436 g of butter - the familiar pound of butter from a little over a quart of cream. Salt is a share of the churned butter weight and is added after the churn, so it does not change the yield, and commercial salted butter carries about 1.5 to 2 percent. Cream weight is accepted from 50 to 20,000 g, cream fat from 10 to 50 percent, butter fat from 70 to 90 percent, buttermilk fat from 0 to 5 percent and salt from 0 to 3 percent; those ranges already keep the butter fat above the cream fat and the cream fat above the buttermilk fat, so the butter weight is always positive and smaller than the cream. Cream under 30 percent fat, butter under 80 percent milkfat, buttermilk above 2 percent and salt above 2.5 percent each raise a warning rather than a refusal. Churn technique, washing, working and the water left in the butter all shift the real yield, homogenised cream may not churn at all, and nothing is claimed about food safety, shelf life or the standard of identity of the butter made. Weights are rounded to 0.1 g and percentages to one decimal. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: 7 CFR 58.305(a) - Butter: made exclusively from milk or cream, with or without salt, containing not less than 80 percent by weight of milkfat
USDA AMS, Butter Grading Information: butter is produced by churning cream until the fat separates from the liquid buttermilk and contains not less than 80 percent milkfat
